For no one has a mind so blind that they don’t see this themselves, no one’s so dull-witted that they don’t understand, of such stubborn judgement that they don’t recognize that sacred theology has been polluted by these vile fools, and that they have prostituted the heavenly Muses as if they were something profane. ‘Base and insolent souls’ (as indeed Luther calls them somewhere), ‘for the sake of a small profit, they scurry to the tables of nobles and illustrious men, like flies to a milk-pail, in the hope of a benefice’, and rush into any court or city, prepared for any occupation.

lg.l: He is led around … like a wooden puppet by another’s wires …

p.ed:trans: following the morsel, like parrots, they babble out whatever you want in the hope of gain: ‘Obsequious Parasites’ (Erasmus says), ‘they teach, say, write, advise and approve anything you want against their conscience, not for the salvation of their flock, but to contrive their own splendid fortune. They assert any opinions and principles against the word of God, in order not to offend their patron, to retain the favour of the great and the applause of the people, and to amass riches for themselves.’ Indeed, very many of them turn their minds to theology not as a divine matter, but for their own purpose; not to advance the good of the Church, but to pillage it; seeking, as Paul says, ‘not the things of Jesus Christ, but their own things’, they gather not the treasure of the lord, but treasure for themselves and their families. Nor is this only the practice of those of meaner fortune and humbler rank: this evil has seized the middle and upper classes, exalted men, not to say bishops.

lg.l: Tell us, pontiffs, what’s gold doing amongst sacred things?

p.ed:trans:
‘Greed often leads the most eminent men astray’, and those who outshine others with their upright character; they lead the way to simony, and dashing against this rock of corruption, not only shear the flock but flay it, and wherever they go, they pillage, drain, extort, making a shipwreck of their reputation, if not their souls: so the evil seems to have spread not from the bottom to the top, but from the top to the bottom, and that which someone once joked is true, ‘What he first bought, he can rightly sell.’ ‘For the simoniac’ (I say this with Leo) ‘hasn’t received a favour, and if he doesn’t receive it, he doesn’t have it, and if he doesn’t have it, he can’t be grateful’; in fact, some of those who sit at the helm are so far from promoting others that they thoroughly obstruct them, being very well aware of the skills by which they attained their own position. ‘For he who believes that he has risen because of his learning is a fool: he who thinks that it’s the reward for actual genius, erudition, experience, honesty, piety, and devotion to the Muses’ (which once was true, and today is only expected) ‘is most clearly insane.’ However or from wherever this evil originated, I shall not further enquire; from these beginnings arose the foulest vices, every calamity, all the multitude of miseries that assail the Church. Hence such frequent simony, hence the complaints that
have arisen, the deceits, the impostures; every wickedness derives from this source. I shall not speak, by the way, of ambition, of flattery greater than in courts (in order that they don’t suffer a dismal dinner at home), of luxury, of the sometimes loathsome example of their life, by which they offend a good many, of their sybaritic drinking, etc. Hence that academic squalor, ‘the sorrow of the Muses in these times’, when any petty man ignorant of the arts can rise by these skills, be promoted and grow rich in this way, be distinguished with ostentatious titles, be venerable with many dignities and dazzle the eyes of the masses, and revel in it, strutting around loftily and exhibiting a certain grandeur and extraordinary punctiliousness, with a venerable beard, an elegant gown, gleaming in purple, and attracting the most attention for his magnificent household and numerous servants. ‘Like the statues’ (as {Budaeus} says) ‘placed on columns in sacred buildings, which look as if they are giving way under their load, and sweating, when in truth they have no feeling, and add nothing to the strength of the stone’, they want to seem Atlases, when they are actually stony statues, shadowy little men, dolts perhaps and dullards, no different from rock. Meanwhile, men who are learned and endowed with the graces of a more holy life, who endure the heat of the day, by unjust fate serve these men; content perhaps with a tiny salary, addressed with simple titles, humble, obscure – although much more worthy – destitute and unrewarded, they lead their own private lives, entombed in poor parishes, or incarcerated forever in their colleges, and lie hidden without fame. But I don’t want to stir up this filthy water any more; hence these tears, the Muses being in mourning, hence religion itself (as I say with Sesellius) ‘is led into ridicule and contempt’, the priesthood degraded; and this being so, I dare to say (borrowing the rotten saying of a rotten fellow about the clergy) they are ‘a rotten mob’: mean, coarse, squalid, melancholy, miserable, despicable, contemptible.]
